tier_reason: README Performance section gives Google Benchmark 1.9.1 code in benchmarks/ (bench_pool.cpp, bench_stack.cpp, bench_freelist.cpp, bench_threadsafe_pool.cpp) against operator new/delete and malloc/free, with GCC 14.2.0, -O3 -march=native (FAST_ALLOC_NATIVE_ARCH=ON), AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE, pinned CPU and 7 repetitions; the Linux row alone meets A. The macOS and Windows rows are single CI repetitions on runners with no CPU model given.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux (GCC 14.2.0, Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE): pool allocate/free 2.00 ns vs 6.03 ns new/delete (3.0x); stack allocate/reset 1.99 vs 4.77 ns malloc/free (2.4x); stack 1,000-allocation frame 1205 vs 14385 ns (11.9x); free-list first-fit 4.66 vs 4.67 ns (1.0x); best-fit 0.76x and thread-safe pool 0.60x (slower). The larger ratios are from single-repetition CI runs against weaker system allocators: Windows MSVC pool 14.9x, stack 20.1x/24.0x, free-list 6.7x; macOS pool 4.0x, stack 4.7x/7.0x, free-list 2.2x/1.7x.
corrections.caveats: Compares special-purpose pool, stack and free-list arenas, preallocated outside the timed loop, with the general system allocator, a weak baseline; no jemalloc or mimalloc comparison. On Linux the free-list matches malloc (first-fit) or is slower (best-fit, 0.76x), and the thread-safe pool is slower than new/delete on one thread (0.60x). The recorded malloc frame benchmark also allocated and released a pointer array inside the timed loop, which inflates the frame speedups (README says the setup has since changed and fresh results are not comparable). macOS and Windows tables are one CI repetition at 0.1 s minimum time on GitHub-hosted runners with no CPU model. Native CPU optimisation became opt-in on 2026-10-04, after the recorded run. 0 stars; not run.

notes: Numbers match the README tables exactly; the record's headline ranges mix the Linux run with the much larger Windows CI ratios, so claimed_speedup now separates them. baseline_stdlib widened because the three tables cover GCC/libstdc++, Apple Clang/libc++ and MSVC STL operator new.

tier_reason: docs/garbage_collector/benchmarks.md compares SGCL with std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr (plus Go and Java ZGC) using the public benchmarks/ programs and benchmarks/run.sh and compare.sh, built with Apple clang 21.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG on an Apple M2 Ultra; code, compiler, flags and CPU are all stated.

corrections.caveats: The docs deliberately leave the Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC out of the tables, so there is no head-to-head with Boehm GC. The malloc behind unique_ptr/shared_ptr is the macOS nano zone, not glibc, jemalloc or mimalloc (an earlier run with MallocNanoZone=0 made those columns about a quarter slower). C++ columns are from a 4 October 2026 run at -O3; the Go and Java columns are from 19 September 2026, when the C++ side was built at -O2, and were not rerun. Apple Silicon only; no number reproduced on x86-64, Linux or Windows yet. SGCL is slower than unique_ptr for 256 B objects on 24 threads (71.4 vs 23.5 ns), copies a pointer slower than a raw pointer (1.4-1.9 vs 0.6 ns), and uses more memory than unique_ptr in binary-trees (292 vs 134 MB at depth 21). The wall-time wins move destruction to the collector thread, so process CPU time is closer (binary-trees depth 21: 9.41 vs 12.39 s CPU).

notes: All allocation numbers in claimed_speedup match the Allocation table. The page also shows binary-trees depth 21 at 4.43 s vs 12.42 s unique_ptr and 14.40 s shared_ptr, and shared_ptr drop-all of 68-171 ms vs microseconds for SGCL. baseline_stdlib set to libc++ because Apple clang on macOS uses libc++ (inferred from the toolchain, not stated on the page).

tier_reason: README Cross-allocator comparison runs the in-tree bench/mb_01..mb_06 programs via scripts/bench-compare.sh with LD_PRELOAD of Debian Trixie glibc, jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc; v8malloc built as a clang Release build with -flto=auto, on an Intel Core Ultra 5 236V. Code, compiler, flags and CPU are stated (the clang version is not), so A is kept at the margin.

corrections.claimed_speedup: MB-02 64 B scalability: 4 threads 150.5 M ops/s vs 134.9 glibc, 122.6 tcmalloc, 124.1 jemalloc, 102.6 mimalloc (12% over glibc); 8 threads 296.4 M vs 295.2 glibc, 290.8 tcmalloc, 271.3 jemalloc, 217.5 mimalloc (within noise of glibc and tcmalloc); MB-01 8 B 22 ns/op vs 23 glibc and tcmalloc, 26 jemalloc, 32 mimalloc; MB-06 256 MiB alloc p99 1 us vs 48 glibc, 8 jemalloc, 2 tcmalloc, 160 mimalloc; MB-05 RSS 9.13 MiB, tied with glibc, vs 19.50 tcmalloc and 27.50 jemalloc. Slower on MB-01 16-256 KiB (59-62 vs 24 ns tcmalloc), MB-03 producer/consumer and MB-04 mixed (11.50 vs 22.26 M tcmalloc, 15.42 M glibc).
corrections.caveats: Each cell is a single run in an 8-core dev container, and the README itself says to treat single-digit-percent gaps as noise, which covers most of the wins (8-thread MB-02 is 0.4% over glibc, MB-01 small sizes within 1 ns). The clear wins are MB-02 at 4 threads, 256 MiB p99 latency and fragmentation RSS. The README shows it behind tcmalloc and glibc on the mixed workload (11.50 vs 22.26 and 15.42 M ops/s), about 2.5x slower than tcmalloc on 16-256 KiB allocations, and behind mimalloc and glibc on producer/consumer. Clang version not stated; README's make release target uses GCC while the table used clang. Status line says most allocator internals are still being implemented, and this run included a concurrency bug fix in v8m_core_cache_pop_batch (MB-03 SEGV). Linux only. 1 star; not run.

notes: All numbers in the record appear in the README tables. claimed_speedup now leads with the 4-thread result, since the 8-thread margin the record led with is inside the author's own noise band. Glibc is the default here, and the README gives baseline numbers for all four incumbents.
